passages.t: The sword of the LORD drawn
passages.happening:
God tells Ezekiel to set his face toward Jerusalem and prophesy against the sanctuary and the land. ‘I am against you, and I will draw My sword from its sheath and cut off from you both the righteous and the wicked’ (verse 3), from south to north (verse 4).

“But you, son of man, groan! Groan before their eyes with a broken heart and bitter grief” (verse 6). When people ask why, he is to say it is because of the news that is coming, when every heart will melt and every knee turn to water (verse 7). Then comes the Song of the Sword: ‘A sword, a sword, sharpened and polished’ (verse 9), made ready for slaughter and given into the hand of the slayer (verses 9-17).
passages.hearers:
In Hebrew Bibles these verses are numbered 21:6 to 22, since 20:45-49 there begins chapter 21.

The chapter belongs to the years around Zedekiah's revolt against Babylon, shortly before Nebuchadnezzar marched west in 589 or 588 BC. Zedekiah had sworn loyalty to Babylon but joined a coalition of small western states in rebellion.

Groaning in public, striking the thigh and clapping the hands were gestures of grief and alarm, here acted out as signs. The Song of the Sword is a war poem, with short, repeated, sharp lines, made to sound like the thing it describes.
passages.later: Envoys from Edom, Moab, Ammon, Tyre and Sidon came to Zedekiah to plan revolt (Jeremiah 27:3). Jeremiah also told of the sword coming on the land (Jeremiah 12:12).
passages.hard:
How can God say his sword will cut off both the righteous and the wicked, when chapter 18 said each person answers for his own sin?

The tension is real and sits a few pages apart in the same book. Several answers are given. One is that the two chapters speak of different things. Chapter 18 concerns a person's standing before God, life or death as God's verdict; chapter 21 describes the disaster of war, in which the innocent and the guilty of a city suffer together. Another notes that the ancient Greek translation reads unrighteous and lawless in verse 3, which suggests that some ancient readers were uneasy with the Hebrew. A third hears the phrase as a way of saying everyone, as English speaks of young and old.

What the chapter does not say is that God regards the righteous and the wicked alike in the end. The book shows God marking those who grieve over the city's sins (9:4) and preserving a remnant. War falls on all; God's final judgment does not treat all as the same. And no one's suffering in war is here made a sign of their guilt.
passages.asks: Ezekiel was told to groan before the people with a broken heart. Ask whether you can speak of judgment without grief. And ask what it would mean to weep before you warn.

passages.t: The king at the fork in the road
passages.happening:
God tells Ezekiel to mark two roads for the sword of the king of Babylon, one to Rabbah of the Ammonites and one to Jerusalem (verses 19-20). ‘For the king of Babylon stands at the fork in the road, at the junction of the two roads, to seek an omen: He shakes the arrows, he consults the idols, he examines the liver’ (verse 21). The lot falls on Jerusalem, where he will set up battering rams and build a siege wall (verse 22).

To Judah's wicked prince God says, ‘Remove the turban, and take off the crown. Things will not remain as they are: Exalt the lowly and bring low the exalted’ (verse 26). “A ruin, a ruin, I will make it a ruin! And it will not be restored until the arrival of Him to whom it belongs” (verse 27). A last word of the sword falls on the Ammonites (verses 28-32).
passages.hearers:
Verse 21 is a precise picture of Babylonian divination. Shaking arrows meant marking arrows with names and drawing one out. The idols were household images used to seek omens. Examining the liver of a sacrificed sheep was the most prestigious method in Babylon; clay models of livers inscribed with omens for students have been found. The pagan king uses every pagan method, and the God of Israel guides the result.

Ammon and Judah were both rebels, and Nebuchadnezzar had to choose which to strike first. He chose Jerusalem. Rabbah lies under modern Amman.

Verse 27 is widely heard as an echo of Jacob's words over Judah, that the scepter will not depart until the one comes to whom it belongs. Jewish and Christian interpreters alike have read it of the Messiah, and Christians see it in Jesus, the son of David. The kingship taken from Zedekiah is held in trust for its rightful heir.
passages.later: Jacob said, ‘The scepter will not depart from Judah’ (Genesis 49:10). Hannah sang that God ‘humbles and He exalts’ (1 Samuel 2:7).
passages.asks: God brings the exalted low and lifts the lowly. Ask where you are holding on to a crown that is not yours. And ask what it means that the true king's right is being kept for him.
